packs.title: Mosaics, collections and open paths
packs.promise: Read civic mosaics and collections, make from garden details and take an easy path return.

q.s: Let specimen labels limit the story you tell.
st: Choose three currently readable fossil or fossil-related specimen displays in the public museum. They may share a gallery; no exact named specimen is required.
Make a card for each: the displayed specimen name, one visible feature and one stated time, place or scientific interpretation from its label. Paraphrase the evidence briefly.
Mark which part of each card came from your eyes and which came from the museum. If a specimen is a cast or model and the label says so, keep that distinction.
Arrange the cards in a useful order of your choice and explain that order in two sentences. Add one question you could not answer from the displays alone.

q.s: Read three mechanical objects through their visible parts.
st: Choose three currently visible mechanical artifacts or vehicle parts with readable interpretation in the admitted collection. Stay outside display boundaries.
For each, record the object’s stated identity and one visible part: a linkage, wheel, fin, pipe, opening, spring or other detail you can distinguish.
Use its actual label to record a supported purpose or connection. When the label does not explain your chosen part, write a question rather than inventing its function.
Put the three cards in the order you would use to explain motion, control or heat to a friend. Explain one supported connection and identify one remaining uncertainty.

q.s: Find three ways materials carry an artwork.
st: Choose three currently displayed works with usable medium or material information in the opened public galleries. Different works can share a medium.
Record each work’s stated medium and one visible handling detail, such as a layered edge, glazed surface, woven join, printed mark or brush trace. Describe only what you can see.
Make a short index connecting those details to three descriptive words of your own. Keep the artist’s factual label separate from your response.
Write one question about what would change if one work used a different material. Label that possibility as your own speculation, not the artist’s intention.

packs.title: Downtown and Haymarket in two afternoons
packs.promise: Connect public collections, street details and railway history across two afternoons.

q.s: Build a small history sequence from museum evidence.
st: Choose three current museum objects or display records with readable Nebraska history interpretation. They may come from one public exhibition.
For each, record its named object or subject, one stated date or period, and one visible or labelled detail. Keep an unknown date as a clearly marked question.
Make a three-record sequence in the order supported by the interpretation. Where a precise date is missing, show that uncertainty rather than forcing an invented position.
Write one supported change across the sequence and one question about a person, place or use that the records leave open.

q.s: Read music through books, scores and recording cases.
st: Choose three publicly available music items, using at least two formats if possible: a book, printed score, recording case or reference volume. Do not enter storage or staff areas.
Record each item’s title, creator or performer where stated, and format from the actual cover, spine or catalogue information. Missing metadata can stay a question.
For each, write what kind of question that format could help answer: background, musical structure, recorded performance or another possibility of your own. No listening or copying music is needed.
Arrange your three records into a reading or discovery order and explain why you would start with one. Return handled items as staff directs.

q.s: Translate two facade details into a small original design.
st: From the open public sidewalk, choose two actual facade details: a window outline, brick course, wall opening or other shape visible from your view.
Describe each detail briefly, then simplify it into your own line or shape. Do not reproduce stained-glass imagery or a religious artwork.
Combine your two invented shapes into a three-tile strip in words or a sketch. Change their arrangement or spacing so the strip is an original response rather than a tracing.
Add two notes connecting the shapes to what you observed, and give the strip an original title.
